chapter: The Human Eye And The colorful World
subject: Science

questions.question: On which part of the human eye is the image of an object formed?
questions.explanation: The light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye where a real and inverted image is formed is called the retina.

questions.question: Light enters the human eye through a thin membrane called:
questions.explanation: Light enters the eye through a thin, transparent membrane on the front surface of the eyeball known as the cornea, which acts as the primary refractive surface of the eye.

questions.question: What is the approximate diameter of the human eyeball?
questions.explanation: The human eyeball is approximately spherical in shape with an approximate diameter of about 2.3 cm.

questions.question: Where does the major part of the refraction of light rays entering the human eye occur?
questions.explanation: Light enters the eye through the cornea, and the major portion of the refraction or bending of light rays takes place at the outer surface of the cornea.

questions.question: The change in the focal length of the eye lens to focus on objects at varying distances is caused by the action of the:
questions.explanation: The ciliary muscles modify the curvature of the crystalline lens, which changes its focal length—a process known as power of accommodation.

questions.question: Which dark muscular diaphragm controls the size of the pupil in the human eye?
questions.explanation: The iris is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil, regulating the amount of light entering the eye.

questions.question: Which part of the human eye controls and regulates the amount of light entering the eye by adjusting the size of the pupil?
questions.explanation: The iris is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil, thereby regulating and controlling the amount of light entering the eye.

questions.question: What are the properties of the image formed on the retina by the eye lens?
questions.explanation: The eye lens forms a real and inverted image of the object on the light-sensitive screen called the retina.

questions.question: Which part of the human eye contains an enormous number of light-sensitive cells that generate electrical signals when light falls on them?
questions.explanation: The retina is a delicate membrane containing an enormous number of light-sensitive cells (rods and cones) that convert light energy into electrical signals sent to the brain.

questions.question: Which nerve transmits the electrical signals generated by light-sensitive cells from the retina to the brain?
questions.explanation: The light-sensitive cells of the retina generate electrical signals when light falls on them, and these signals are then transmitted to the brain via the optic nerve.

questions.question: When the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the eye lens becomes thin, which enables us to see:
options: Only objects at a very close distance
questions.explanation: When the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the eye lens becomes thin, which increases its focal length and allows us to focus on and see distant objects clearly.

questions.question: When the ciliary muscles contract, what change occurs in the eye lens to help us see nearby objects clearly?
options: The eye lens becomes thin and its focal length increases.
The eye lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases.
The eye lens remains completely rigid and unchanged.
The eye lens flattens and stops refracting light.
questions.explanation: When we view nearby objects, the ciliary muscles contract, which causes the curvature of the eye lens to increase, making it thicker. This decreases its focal length so that the image is properly focused on the retina.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'accommodation' of the human eye?
options: The ability of the iris to control the amount of light entering the pupil
The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to focus on objects at varying distances
The process by which the retina converts light into electrical signals
The ability of the cornea to perform the major refraction of light
questions.explanation: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length using the ciliary muscles so as to clearly focus objects at varying distances on the retina is called accommodation.

questions.question: What is the least distance of distinct vision for a normal human eye?
questions.explanation: The minimum distance at which objects can be seen most distinctly without any strain is called the least distance of distinct vision, and for a normal human eye, it is 25 cm.

questions.question: What is defined as the minimum distance at which an object can be seen most distinctly without any strain on the eye?
options: Radius of curvature of the cornea
Focal length of the eye lens
questions.explanation: The least distance of distinct vision (or near point of the eye) is the minimum distance at which an object can be seen most clearly and distinctly without strain, which is 25 cm for a normal human eye.

questions.question: What is the near point of the human eye?
options: The maximum distance up to which the eye can see objects clearly, which is infinity.
The minimum distance from the eye at which an object can be seen most distinctly without strain, which is 25 cm for a normal eye.
The exact distance between the cornea and the retina.
The focal length of the crystalline lens when the ciliary muscles are fully relaxed.
questions.explanation: The near point of the eye (also called the least distance of distinct vision) is defined as the minimum distance from the eye at which an object can be seen most clearly and distinctly without any strain, equal to 25 cm for a normal human eye.

questions.question: What is the far point of a normal human eye?
questions.explanation: The far point of the eye is the farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly, and for a normal human eye, it is infinity.

questions.question: What is the medical condition in older people where the crystalline lens of the eye becomes milky and cloudy, leading to a partial or complete loss of vision?
questions.explanation: Cataract is the condition where the crystalline lens of elderly people becomes milky and cloudy due to the formation of a membrane over it, causing partial or complete loss of vision, which can be corrected through surgery.

questions.question: Which other name is commonly used for the vision defect known as myopia?
questions.explanation: Myopia is also known as nearsightedness. A person with myopia can see nearby objects clearly, but cannot see distant objects distinctly.

questions.question: A person suffering from myopia (nearsightedness) cannot clearly see:
options: Objects kept at the near point
questions.explanation: A person with myopia can see nearby objects clearly, but cannot see distant objects distinctly because the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina rather than on it.

questions.question: Where is the image of a distant object formed in the eye of a person suffering from myopia (nearsightedness)?
questions.explanation: In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina rather than directly on it, which is why distant objects appear blurred.

questions.question: What are the two main causes or conditions that can lead to myopia (nearsightedness)?
options: Excessive curvature of the eye lens and elongation of the eyeball
Flattening of the eye lens and shortening of the eyeball
Clouding of the crystalline lens and weakening of the iris
Decrease in the focal length of the cornea and loss of ciliary muscle elasticity
questions.explanation: Myopia is caused by either (1) excessive curvature of the eye lens or (2) elongation of the eyeball. Both of these conditions result in the image of a distant object being formed in front of the retina.

questions.question: Which type of lens is used to correct the vision defect known as myopia (nearsightedness)?
questions.explanation: Myopia is corrected by using a concave lens of suitable power, which diverges the incoming light rays so that they are focused on the retina.

questions.question: Which of the following vision defects is also known as farsightedness?
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is commonly known as farsightedness. A person with hypermetropia can see distant objects clearly, but cannot see nearby objects distinctly because the image of a close object is focused behind the retina.

questions.question: Which person or condition describes someone who cannot see distant objects clearly?
options: A person with normal vision looking at infinity
A person suffering from presbyopia only for near objects
questions.explanation: A person suffering from myopia (nearsightedness) can see nearby objects clearly, but cannot see distant objects distinctly because the image is formed in front of the retina.

questions.question: The increase in the near point of the eye (commonly seen in old age or presbyopia) is primarily due to:
options: Elongation of the eyeball and excessive curvature of the cornea
Gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens
Clouding of the crystalline lens membrane
A sudden decrease in the refractive index of the aqueous humor
questions.explanation: As people age, accommodation power decreases due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility (loss of elasticity) of the crystalline lens, causing the near point to recede further away.

questions.question: What are the two main causes of hypermetropia (farsightedness)?
options: Excessive curvature of the eye lens and elongation of the eyeball
The focal length of the eye lens is too long and the eyeball has become too small
Clouding of the crystalline lens and complete loss of accommodation
A sudden decrease in the refractive index of the aqueous humor
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is caused by either (1) the focal length of the eye lens being too long, or (2) the eyeball having become too small, which results in images of nearby objects being focused behind the retina.

questions.question: What are the two main causes of hypermetropia (farsightedness)?
options: Excessive curvature of the eye lens and elongation of the eyeball
The focal length of the eye lens is too long and the eyeball has become too small
Clouding of the crystalline lens and complete loss of accommodation
A sudden decrease in the refractive index of the aqueous humor
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is caused by either (1) the focal length of the eye lens being too long, or (2) the eyeball having become too small, which results in images of nearby objects being focused behind the retina.

questions.question: What is the vision defect known as presbyopia?
options: The inability to see distant objects clearly due to an elongated eyeball
The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with aging, causing the near point to gradually recede
The total clouding of the crystalline lens causing complete blindness
The distortion of vision due to an irregular curvature of the cornea
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the defect of vision arising from old age, where the power of accommodation of the eye decreases due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens, making it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably.

questions.question: What is the primary cause of presbyopia?
options: Excessive elongation of the eyeball and a very thick lens
Gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens
The formation of a milky membrane over the cornea
A sudden decrease in the distance between the lens and the retina
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is caused by the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and the diminishing flexibility (loss of elasticity) of the crystalline lens as a person ages, reducing the eye's power of accommodation.

questions.question: Which type of lens is commonly used to correct the vision defect known as presbyopia?
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is commonly corrected using bifocal lenses (which contain both concave lenses for viewing distant objects and convex lenses for reading/nearby objects). Simple convex lenses can also be used if the person only needs assistance with close-up vision.

questions.question: Within what time frame after death must the eyes of a donor be removed to ensure successful eye donation?
questions.explanation: Eyes must be removed within 4 to 6 hours after death to ensure the donated corneas remain viable for transplantation.

questions.question: Which of the following individuals or persons with specific conditions CANNOT donate their eyes?
options: A person who has diabetes or hypertension
A person who wore spectacles or had cataract surgery
A person who died of AIDS, rabies, cholera, or acute leukemia
A person who is over 70 years old
questions.explanation: Eyes cannot be donated by persons who have died from communicable or infectious diseases such as AIDS, hepatitis B or C, rabies, cholera, acute leukemia, tetanus, or infectious brain diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, as these can transmit infections to the recipient.

questions.question: What is the angle of a prism?
options: The angle between the refracting surfaces of the prism Or angle of rectrangle surfaces
The angle at which light enters the base of the prism
The angle of deviation between the incident ray and emergent ray
The angle between the base and the top edge of the prism
questions.explanation: The angle between the two refracting surfaces of a glass prism is called the angle of the prism (or refracting angle).

questions.question: What is an incident ray in optics?
options: The ray of light that strikes or falls on a reflecting or refracting surface
The ray of light that bounces off a mirror after reflection
The ray of light that emerges out of a prism or lens
The ray of light that travels parallel to the principal axis
questions.explanation: An incident ray is the ray of light that falls upon or strikes a surface (such as a mirror, lens, or prism) before reflection or refraction takes place.

questions.question: What is a refracted ray in optics?
options: The ray of light that bounces back into the first medium after striking a reflective surface
The ray of light that travels into the second medium after changing its direction at the boundary between two transparent media
The ray of light that passes straight through a medium without any change in speed or path
The ray of light that travels strictly perpendicular along the normal line
questions.explanation: When light travels obliquely from one transparent medium into another, it bends at the boundary separating the two media. The ray of light that continues its journey through the second medium is called the refracted ray.

questions.question: What is an emergent ray in optics?
options: The ray of light that strikes the first refracting surface of a prism
The ray of light that travels inside a medium parallel to the normal
The ray of light that emerges or comes out of a transparent medium after refraction
The ray of light that is totally reflected back into the first medium
questions.explanation: An emergent ray is the final ray of light that comes out (or emerges) into the surrounding medium after passing through and undergoing refraction in an optical device like a glass slab or a prism.

questions.question: What is the angle of incidence in optics?
options: The angle between the incident ray and the reflecting or refracting surface
The angle between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is defined as the angle formed between the incident ray and the normal (the perpendicular line drawn to the surface) at the point where the light ray strikes the surface.

questions.question: What is the angle of refraction in optics?
options: The angle between the incident ray and the normal
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence
The angle between the emergent ray and the refracting surface
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray
questions.explanation: The angle of refraction is defined as the angle between the refracted ray and the normal (perpendicular line drawn to the surface) at the point where the light ray enters the second medium.

questions.question: What is the angle of emergence in optics?
options: The angle between the emergent ray and the refracting surface
The angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the point of emergence
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal inside the medium
questions.explanation: The angle of emergence is defined as the angle between the emergent ray and the normal (perpendicular line) drawn at the surface where the light ray exits or emerges from a transparent medium into the surrounding air.

questions.question: What is the angle of emergence in optics?
options: The angle between the emergent ray and the refracting surface
The angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the point of emergence
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal inside the medium
questions.explanation: The angle of emergence is defined as the angle between the emergent ray and the normal (perpendicular line) drawn at the surface where the light ray exits or emerges from a transparent medium into the surrounding air.

questions.question: What is the angle of deviation in optics when a ray of light passes through a prism?
options: The angle between the two refracting surfaces of the prism
The angle between the incident ray (produced forward) and the emergent ray (produced backward)
The angle between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence
The angle between the refracted ray and the base of the prism
questions.explanation: The angle of deviation is the angle between the direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray, representing how much the light ray has been bent from its original path as it passes through the prism.

questions.question: When a ray of light travels from an optically rarer (lighter) medium to a denser medium, in which direction does it bend?
options: It passes straight without any deviation
questions.explanation: When light travels from an optically rarer (lighter) medium to a denser medium, its speed decreases, causing it to bend towards the normal.

questions.question: When a ray of light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer (lighter) medium, in which direction does it bend?
options: It passes straight without any deviation
Along the surface separating the two media
questions.explanation: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium, its speed increases, causing it to bend away from the normal.

questions.question: What is the acronym or short form used to remember the sequence of colors in the spectrum created by the dispersion of white light?
questions.explanation: The spectrum of white light consists of seven colors: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, and Red, which are commonly remembered by the short form/acronym VIBGYOR.

questions.question: What is a spectrum in optics?
options: The band of distinct colored components of a light beam separated by a prism
The angle formed between the incident ray and the emergent ray
The ray of light that travels straight through a medium without deviation
The point where the normal meets the refracting surface
questions.explanation: A spectrum is the band of distinct colored components (such as VIBGYOR) that is formed when a beam of white light passes through a transparent medium like a glass prism and undergoes dispersion.

questions.question: What is dispersion of light?
options: The bouncing back of light rays from a polished reflecting surface
The splitting of white light into its constituent seven colors when passing through a transparent medium like a prism
The bending of light around the sharp corners of an obstacle
The total internal reflection of light rays inside a denser medium
questions.explanation: Dispersion is the phenomenon of splitting a beam of white light into its constituent seven colors (VIBGYOR) due to the differences in how much each color refracts when passing through a transparent medium like a glass prism.

questions.question: Which color among VIBGYOR bends the highest (has the maximum deviation) when passing through a prism?
questions.explanation: Violet light has the shortest wavelength among the visible spectrum, causing it to travel slower in the glass medium and bend (refract) the most compared to the other colors.

questions.question: Which color among VIBGYOR bends the lowest (has the minimum deviation) when passing through a prism?
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest wavelength among the visible spectrum, causing it to bend (refract) the least compared to the other colors when passing through a prism.
